summary.text: Spiral arms are spiral-shaped regions of enhanced brightness within the galactic disc, and they are a defining feature of spiral galaxies.
They hold more interstellar gas and dust, bright stars and star clusters than the rest of the disk, and can supply 40 to 50% of some galaxies' total light.
Grand design galaxies show two distinct arms across the whole galaxy, while flocculent galaxies show many small arm fragments that are not connected.

facts.label: First identified
facts.value: By Lord Rosse in 1850, in galaxy M51

facts.label: Share of galaxy light
facts.value: Can reach 40 to 50% in some galaxies

facts.label: Origin theories
facts.value: Self-propagating star formation and density wave theory

items.prompt: Astronomers photograph the same spiral galaxy with filters for short, bluish wavelengths, then again with longer, redder ones. How do the arms compare?

options.label: Smoother in the first picture, sharper in the second
The same in both pictures
They vanish completely in the second picture
Sharply defined in the first, smoother and less contrasted in the second

items.explain: In blue and ultraviolet light blue supergiants make the arms well defined, while in red and near-infrared older stars make them smoother and less contrasted.

items.prompt: Some spiral galaxies have an elongated block of stars straddling their center. Where do the arms of such a galaxy begin?

options.label: At the ends of the bar
At the very center of the galaxy
Anywhere along the outer edge of the disc
Along the middle of the bar

items.explain: In barred galaxies the arms originate at the ends of the bar, while in unbarred ones they usually start near the center.

items.prompt: You photograph a galaxy whose arms are a patchwork of many short pieces that do not connect. Which kind of spiral is it?

options.label: Grand design
Multi-armed
Flocculent
Barred

items.explain: Flocculent galaxies have numerous small arm fragments not connected to each other.

items.prompt: Two spiral galaxies are compared: one has tightly wound, smooth arms, the other has knotty, loosely wound arms. How does the Hubble scheme label them?

options.label: Loosely wound is Sa, tightly wound is Sc
Both are labelled Sb
Tightly wound is Sa, loosely wound is Sc
Both share one label and differ only in size

items.explain: Early type Sa and SBa galaxies have tightly wound, smooth arms, while late type Sc and SBc galaxies have knotty, loosely wound arms.

items.prompt: A spiral galaxy's arms look brighter than the rest of its disc. What is packed into them that the rest of the disc has less of?

options.label: More dark matter than anywhere else in the disc
Mostly old red stars and very little gas
Nothing extra; the brightness is only a trick of viewing
More gas and dust, with bright stars and star clusters

items.explain: Arms have an increased concentration of gas and dust, active starburst, and more star clusters and bright stars than the rest of the disk.

items.prompt: Astronomers have two main theories for how spiral arms arise: a star formation model and the density wave theory. A student asks which one has been proven wrong. What is the best answer?

options.label: The density wave theory, since it was replaced
Neither, since they describe different variants and do not rule each other out
The star formation model, since it is the older one
Both, since no theory explains spiral arms

items.explain: The two theories describe different variants of the spiral structure and do not exclude each other.
